docs.answer: Caffeine has a half-life of about **5 hours**, and up to 6 or more in some people, so an afternoon coffee is still partly active at bedtime. It also reduces deep sleep even when you fall asleep fine.

docs.title: Sitting all day
docs.answer: Long uninterrupted sitting is linked to back and neck trouble and worse metabolic health. The fix is frequent movement rather than a perfect posture: stand or walk for a few minutes every half hour and vary how you sit.

docs.title: Headphone volume and hearing
docs.answer: Sustained exposure above about **85 decibels** risks hearing damage, and earbuds at high volume easily exceed that. The practical rule is the 60/60 one: no more than 60% volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time.

docs.title: Left-handedness
docs.answer: About **10%** of people are left-handed. Handedness comes from a mix of genetics and early development rather than a single gene, and it is not a sign of anything else about intelligence.

docs.title: Hiccups
docs.answer: Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm followed by a sudden closure of the vocal cords. They usually stop on their own; slow breathing, sipping water or holding your breath can interrupt the cycle.

docs.title: Sneezing
docs.answer: A sneeze clears irritants from the nasal passages, triggered by nerves in the nose. Most people close their eyes reflexively, but nothing bursts if you keep them open; the pressure simply takes another path.

docs.title: Food and concentration
docs.answer: Stable blood sugar helps attention, so meals with protein, fibre and slow carbohydrates beat a sugar spike. Hydration matters too: mild dehydration reliably worsens concentration and mood before you feel thirsty.

docs.title: Tallest building
docs.answer: The **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai is the tallest building at **828 metres** with 163 floors. It has held the record since 2010.

docs.title: Largest island
docs.answer: **Greenland** is the largest island, at about 2.2 million square kilometres. Australia is larger but is classed as a continent rather than an island, which is a convention more than a physical rule.

docs.title: Number of countries
docs.answer: The usual figure is **195**: 193 member states of the United Nations plus two observer states, the Vatican and Palestine. Some territories and disputed regions are counted differently, which is why you also see numbers like 193 or 197.

docs.title: Roman numerals
docs.answer: Roman numerals use **I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1,000**. Symbols are added left to right, except when a smaller symbol comes before a larger one: IV is 4, IX is 9, XL is 40, and CM is 900. So 2024 is MMXXIV.

docs.title: Binary numbers
docs.answer: Binary is base 2: each place is worth twice the one to its right, using only 0 and 1. So **1011** means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11**. Computers use it because a switch has two reliable states, on and off, which is far easier to build and detect than ten distinct voltage levels.

docs.title: Pi
docs.answer: **Pi** is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about **3.14159**. It appears wherever circles, waves or rotations do. It is irrational, so its decimal never ends or repeats; for almost any real calculation, a handful of digits is plenty.

docs.title: Golden ratio
docs.answer: The **golden ratio** is about **1.618**, the proportion where the whole relates to the larger part as the larger part relates to the smaller. It is the limit of ratios of consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Claims that it explains all of art and nature are often exaggerated, but it genuinely shows up in some growth patterns and tilings.

docs.title: Speed of sound
docs.answer: Sound travels at about **343 metres per second** in air at 20 °C, roughly 1,235 km/h. It moves faster in water and much faster in steel, because the particles are packed closer. Mach 1 means the speed of sound; the delay between lightning and thunder is the same difference, about three seconds per kilometre.

docs.title: Light-year
docs.answer: A **light-year** is a distance, not a time: the distance light travels in one year, about **9.46 trillion kilometres**. Astronomers use it because space is huge and kilometres become unwieldy. The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

docs.title: Absolute zero
docs.answer: Absolute zero is **-273.15 °C**, or 0 kelvin, the point where a system has the least possible thermal energy. You cannot reach it exactly: cooling something requires removing heat, and the closer you get, the harder the last bit is to remove. Particles still have quantum zero-point motion at that temperature.

docs.title: Size of the Earth
docs.answer: Earth's circumference around the equator is about **40,075 km**, and its mean diameter is about **12,742 km**. It bulges slightly at the equator because of rotation, so the polar diameter is about 43 km smaller.

docs.title: Auroras
docs.answer: Charged particles from the Sun stream toward Earth and are funnelled by the magnetic field toward the poles. There they collide with gas in the upper atmosphere, exciting it, and the gas releases the energy as light. **Oxygen** glows green and red; **nitrogen** gives blue and purple. Auroras are strongest near the poles and during high solar activity.

docs.title: Meteor showers
docs.answer: A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through debris left by a comet or asteroid. The grains hit the atmosphere at tens of kilometres per second, heat up and burn, and we see a streak. A **shooting star** is not a star at all, just a small piece of rock or dust.

docs.title: The North Star
docs.answer: **Polaris** sits almost directly above Earth's north pole, so it barely moves while the rest of the sky rotates around it. That makes it useful for finding north in the northern hemisphere. It is not the brightest star, only about the 48th, and it is a multiple star system about 430 light-years away.

docs.title: Déjà vu
docs.answer: Déjà vu is the strong feeling that a new situation has happened before, without being able to place it. The leading explanations involve a brief mismatch in memory processing, where familiarity is triggered without the recollection that normally goes with it. It is common, especially when tired, and usually harmless; frequent episodes alongside other symptoms are worth a doctor's opinion.

docs.title: Muscle memory
docs.answer: **Muscle memory** is motor learning, not memory stored in muscle. Repeated practice builds and prunes connections in the brain, especially the cerebellum and motor cortex, so a movement becomes automatic and needs less conscious attention. The muscles change too, but the skill itself lives in the nervous system, which is why it comes back quickly after a long break.

docs.title: Shivering
docs.answer: Shivering is rapid, involuntary muscle contraction that produces heat as a by-product, a way for the body to defend its core temperature. It is triggered when the hypothalamus decides you are losing heat too fast. With a fever, the set point rises, so you feel cold and shiver until the body reaches the new target.

docs.title: Vitamin D
docs.answer: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium and is needed for healthy bones and muscles. Skin makes it from **UVB sunlight**, and only a few foods contain much. People with dark skin, little sun exposure or who cover up are more likely to be low; a blood test is the way to know, and supplements should be dosed sensibly rather than guessed at large amounts.

docs.title: Vitamin C
docs.answer: Vitamin C is needed to build collagen, the protein in skin, blood vessels and bone, and it helps the body absorb iron. A severe lack causes **scurvy**, with bleeding gums and slow healing. Citrus, peppers, broccoli and kiwi are rich sources. For most people it does not prevent colds, though it may slightly shorten one.

docs.title: Allergies
docs.answer: An allergy is the immune system treating a harmless protein, such as pollen or peanut protein, as a threat. It produces **IgE** antibodies, and the next exposure triggers cells to release **histamine**, causing sneezing, itching, swelling or wheezing. Antihistamines block histamine receptors and reduce the symptoms. Some childhood allergies fade, others persist, and severe reactions need urgent medical help.

docs.title: Viruses and bacteria
docs.answer: Bacteria are single-celled organisms that can live and reproduce on their own, and most are harmless or useful. Viruses are much smaller packages of genetic material that need a host cell to copy themselves. **Antibiotics** target bacterial machinery, so they do nothing against viruses. That is why a cold, which is usually viral, does not improve with antibiotics.

docs.title: The common cold
docs.answer: Colds are caused by many different viruses, most often **rhinoviruses**, which is why there is no single vaccine or cure. Symptoms usually peak in two to three days and clear within about a week to ten. Rest, fluids and simple symptom relief help; antibiotics do not. See a doctor if symptoms last much longer, or if breathing becomes difficult.

docs.title: Fever
docs.answer: A fever is a raised body temperature, usually above about **38 °C**, and it is a controlled response that makes it harder for some germs to multiply. Normal temperature varies by person and time of day. A mild fever is often best left to do its job with fluids and rest; babies, pregnant people and anyone with a very high or persistent fever should get medical advice.

docs.title: Alcohol and sleep
docs.answer: Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster, which is why it feels like a nightcap helps, but it fragments sleep later in the night and suppresses **REM** sleep. It also relaxes the muscles of the airway, worsening snoring and sleep apnoea. The result is a shorter, lighter night even when the total hours look fine.

docs.title: Screens before bed
docs.answer: Screens affect sleep two ways: the content keeps your attention and delays bedtime, and bright light near the eyes can shift the body clock. Blue-light filters reduce one part but do not fix the arousal from messages, games or videos. The reliable fix is putting the phone out of reach for the last 30 to 60 minutes before bed.

docs.title: Napping
docs.answer: A **10 to 20 minute** nap improves alertness without grogginess. Longer naps let you enter deep sleep, and waking from that leaves sleep inertia for a while. Early afternoon is the easiest time to nap because of a natural dip in alertness; napping late in the day can make it harder to fall asleep at night.

docs.title: Daily steps
docs.answer: The 10,000 figure started as a marketing number, not a medical threshold. Large studies link lower mortality with walking, with benefits rising up to roughly **7,000 to 8,000 steps a day** and flattening after that. Any increase from a very low baseline helps, and brisk walking counts more than a slow stroll.

docs.title: Muscle soreness
docs.answer: Delayed onset muscle soreness usually peaks **24 to 72 hours** after unfamiliar or intense exercise. It comes from microscopic damage and the repair response, not from lactic acid, which clears within hours. Soreness is not a reliable measure of a good session; light movement, sleep and protein help recovery, and sharp pain during exercise is a reason to stop.

docs.title: Emergency fund
docs.answer: An emergency fund covers essential expenses if income stops or a large unexpected bill lands. The common target is **three to six months** of necessities, more if your income is irregular or you support others. Keep it somewhere safe and easy to reach, such as a savings account, rather than in investments that can fall just when you need them.

docs.title: Email etiquette
docs.answer: Put the ask in the subject line or the first sentence, keep the body to a few short paragraphs, and make the next action obvious. One email should carry one request. Reply within a working day when you can, use reply-all sparingly, and avoid sarcasm that text cannot carry. If a thread has gone back and forth more than twice, a short call usually saves time.

docs.title: HTTP status codes
docs.answer: HTTP status codes group by first digit: **2xx** success, **3xx** redirect, **4xx** the client's request is wrong, **5xx** the server failed. Common ones: 200 OK, 301 moved permanently, 400 bad request, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests, 500 internal error. A 400 means fix the request; a 500 means the server should be fixed.

docs.title: null and undefined
docs.answer: In JavaScript, **undefined** usually means a value was never assigned, and it is what you get from a missing property or an omitted argument. **null** is an explicit "no value" that a programmer sets on purpose. `typeof null` returning `'object'` is a long-standing bug kept for compatibility. TypeScript's strict null checks make the distinction useful rather than annoying.

docs.title: Flexbox and grid
docs.answer: **Flexbox** lays items out along one axis, a row or a column, and is best for a toolbar, a card's internal layout or distributing space between items. **Grid** defines rows and columns at the same time, and is best for page-level layouts and anything that needs alignment in two directions. They compose well: use grid for the page and flexbox inside the components.

docs.title: SQL joins
docs.answer: A join combines rows from two tables on a matching condition. **INNER JOIN** keeps only rows with a match in both tables. **LEFT JOIN** keeps every row from the left table and fills unmatched right columns with null; **RIGHT JOIN** is the mirror. **FULL OUTER JOIN** keeps unmatched rows from both sides. Most reporting bugs come from an inner join silently dropping rows you expected to keep.

docs.title: Database indexes
docs.answer: An index is a sorted side structure, usually a **B-tree**, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Reads that filter or sort on the indexed column get much faster. The cost is space and slower writes, because every insert, update and delete must update the index too, so index the columns you actually query rather than everything.

docs.title: API key safety
docs.answer: Anything shipped to a browser can be read, so an API key in frontend code or a public repository is already leaked. Keep keys on the server, load them from environment variables or a secret store, and give each one the narrowest scope possible. If a key has been exposed, rotate it rather than hoping nobody noticed; bots scan public repositories within minutes.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication
docs.answer: Two-factor authentication asks for something you know, like a password, plus something you have or are, like a code from an app or a security key. That means a stolen password alone is not enough. Authenticator apps and hardware keys are safer than SMS, which can be intercepted or hijacked through SIM swapping, but any second factor beats none.

docs.title: VPNs
docs.answer: A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN server, so your local network and internet provider cannot read it or see which sites you visit. It does not make you anonymous: the VPN provider can see your traffic, and sites still recognise logins, cookies and browser fingerprints. It is most useful on untrusted networks and for hiding traffic from a local network operator.

docs.title: Browser cookies
docs.answer: A cookie is a small piece of data a site asks your browser to store and send back on later requests. **Session cookies** disappear when the browser closes and keep you logged in; **persistent cookies** have an expiry and remember preferences. First-party cookies are usually functional, while third-party tracking cookies are the ones privacy rules target. Blocking all cookies tends to break logins and carts.

docs.title: Parts of a URL
docs.answer: A URL has a **scheme** (`https`), a **host** (`example.com`), an optional **port**, a **path** (`/blog/post`), an optional **query string** (`?page=2&sort=new`) and an optional **fragment** (`#section`) that points inside the page. The query string is data sent to the server; the fragment is handled by the browser and never sent in the request.

docs.title: Backups
docs.answer: The **3-2-1 rule** is a good default: keep three copies of important data, on two different kinds of media, with one copy off-site. A backup you have never restored is only a hope, so test a restore occasionally. Synchronising to a cloud drive is not a full backup, because a deletion or ransomware infection gets synced too.

docs.title: Git merge and rebase
docs.answer: **Merge** joins two branches and keeps the real history, adding a merge commit. **Rebase** replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a straight line, but it rewrites commit hashes. Rebase your own local branch before sharing it; once commits are pushed and others may have built on them, merge instead, or you will force everyone to reconcile rewritten history.

docs.title: Semantic versioning
docs.answer: Semantic versioning uses **major.minor.patch**. Patch increases for backward-compatible bug fixes, minor for backward-compatible features, and major for breaking changes. A version like `2.4.1` is therefore the second major line, fourth feature release, first patch. Pre-release labels such as `3.0.0-beta.1` sort before the final release.
